title: Rapid Charge Stability Diagram Generation from Device-level Modeling of Semiconductor Quantum Dots
authors: Ron Nodel, David W. Kanaar, Connor Nasseraddin, Tim J. Wilson, Hong-Wen Jiang, Jason R. Petta, Chris Anderson, Mark F. Gyure
abstract: Self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson calculations are a powerful tool for predicting the behavior of layered semiconductor quantum dot devices. However, characterization of charge stability diagrams through fully simulated gate-voltage sweeps is computationally expensive. Combining a Multi-Domain Multi-Model (MDMM) approach with an automated tuning routine, we identify gate voltages associated with selected charge configurations. This small set of self-consistent simulations can be augmented with Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) energy calculations to extract charging energies, lever arms, and interdot Coulomb interactions to directly parameterize a Hubbard model for rapid charge stability diagram generation. For an Intel Tunnel Falls Si/SiGe device, we demonstrate the Hubbard model's ability to reproduce charge stability diagrams at a fraction of the computational cost in comparison to voltage bias sweeps. We further compare the simulated diagrams to experimental data and demonstrate qualitative agreement. Our result represents a step towards predictive digital twin models for semiconductor quantum dot devices. Finally, we apply this workflow towards lever arm engineering in a second device, demonstrating that the method extends to multiple architectures.
summary: This work presents a novel, computationally efficient workflow to generate charge stability diagrams for semiconductor quantum dots. By combining advanced device simulations (MDMM/Schrödinger-Poisson) with Full Configuration Interaction calculations, the authors parameterize an effective Hubbard model. This model allows for rapid prediction of device behavior, showing promising agreement with experimental results and paving the way for predictive quantum device modeling.
main_problem: Characterizing charge stability diagrams for semiconductor quantum dot devices is computationally expensive using full gate-voltage sweeps via self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson calculations.
main_result: The derived Hubbard model, parameterized using a combination of MDMM simulations and FCI calculations, successfully reproduces charge stability diagrams with qualitative agreement to experimental data.
method: The authors combine Multi-Domain Multi-Model (MDMM) Schrödinger-Poisson simulations with an automated tuning routine to identify gate voltages, which are then used alongside Full Configuration Interaction (FCI) calculations to parameterize an effective Hubbard model.
model_or_system: The system is a layered semiconductor quantum dot device (e.g., Intel Tunnel Falls Si/SiGe). The physics is modeled using the extended Hubbard Hamiltonian, which captures intra-site and inter-site Coulomb interactions.
key_observables: Charge stability diagrams, charging energies, lever arms, and interdot Coulomb interactions.
important_parameters: Gate voltages ($V_1, V_2$), Hubbard parameters ($U_1, U_2, U_{12}$), and dielectric thicknesses ($	ext{HfO}_2$ variation).
main_assumptions: The method relies on approximating the complex device physics by parameterizing a simplified Hubbard model using a small set of self-consistent simulations and assuming the validity of a constant lever arm matrix.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the device geometry, the application of MDMM subdomains, and the resulting charge stability diagrams comparing theory to experiment.
paper_structure: The paper first establishes the computational bottleneck of full simulations, then details the MDMM/autotuning approach to extract parameters, parameterizes the Hubbard model, and finally validates the model by comparing predictions against experimental charge stability diagrams and testing its applicability to different architectures.
why_interesting: The development of a predictive 'digital twin' model for quantum dot charge states, moving from expensive first-principles simulations to rapid, effective Hamiltonian descriptions, is highly relevant for designing and controlling quantum computing hardware.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. The approximate Tunnel Falls gate geometry and calculated charge density. The gate names are overlayed, with the MDMM subdomains shown by dashed lines around P2 and P3. The two-dimensional charge density associated with one electron in both P2 and P3 (1,1) is shown in the color map and is found using the autotuning procedure described in Section II A, integrated over the quantum well thickness. This is a triple quantum dot tuned up as a double quantum dot, with P1 and B1 acting as accumulation gates, following standard experimental tune-up. Sensor accumulation gates are modeled as smaller for computational efficiency and have minimal effect on the P2-P3 charge stability diagram.
FIG. 2. The schematic layout of the overlapping gate device design with each gate described. Additional information on this device is described in Section III.

FIG. 3. The Intel device charge stability diagrams found using three methods. (a) A Hubbard model parameterized using five autotuned points indicated by blue circles in (b), with an FCI calculation at these points. This parameterized model was then used to generate the rest of the diagram, with the (1,1) charge cell displayed in red. (b) The charge stability diagram obtained by running self-consistent Schrödinger-Poisson simulations at 441 (21 × 21) points in voltage space, with the autotuned points shown as reference. The Thomas–Fermi model overestimates the charging energies relative to the fully quantum model, and the fully quantum model overestimates charging energies relative to the experiment.
